solution.concept_anchor: Absolute bars on judicial review vs. reviewable with limited grounds

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 105(2), a Member of Parliament cannot be held liable in any court for anything said or any vote cast inside Parliament — courts have no jurisdiction to examine such speech.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 105(2) provides absolute parliamentary privilege: members cannot be subjected to any proceedings in any court for anything said in Parliament or for any vote cast there. This is a constitutionally absolute bar on judicial review of parliamentary speech.

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 74(2), courts cannot inquire into the nature of advice given by the Council of Ministers to the President, making such advice entirely immune from judicial scrutiny.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 74(2) expressly bars courts from inquiring into whether or what advice was given by the Council of Ministers — this is one of the rare explicit non-justiciability provisions in the Indian Constitution.

statement_analysis.statement: A Speaker's decision on disqualification under the Tenth Schedule is final and conclusively immune from judicial review in all circumstances.
statement_analysis.reason: In Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992), the Supreme Court held that Paragraph 7 (which sought to bar all judicial review of the Speaker's decisions) violated the Basic Structure. Speaker's orders are reviewable on grounds of mala fides, perversity, or violation of natural justice.

statement_analysis.statement: Presidential proclamation of National Emergency under Article 352 is judicially reviewable if the mandatory procedural requirements introduced by the 44th Constitutional Amendment are not complied with.
statement_analysis.reason: Post-44th Amendment, the procedural requirements — written Cabinet advice, approval by both Houses within one month — are justiciable. Courts can review whether these procedures were followed, even though they do not substitute their judgment on the substantive necessity of the Emergency.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' is a strong distractor because Statement 3 sounds absolute and final — students who know the Speaker's role is powerful and has 'finality' under the Tenth Schedule but who have not studied Kihoto Hollohan precisely will mark Statement 3 as correct, getting four correct and choosing (d) 'All four' or miscounting to reach (c).
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Article 105(2) — absolute parliamentary privilege, no judicial review of speech in Parliament. Correct.
Statement 2: Article 74(2) — express bar on inquiring into ministerial advice. Correct.

Statement 3: Kihoto Hollohan (1992) struck down the absolute finality clause (Paragraph 7) — Speaker's orders ARE reviewable on mala fides, perversity, natural justice grounds. Statement 3 — 'conclusively immune in all circumstances' — is Incorrect.
Statement 4: Post-44th Amendment procedural requirements for Emergency proclamation are justiciable. Correct.
Three statements (1, 2, 4) are correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 uses the 'absolute' and 'all circumstances' qualifier to create a partial-truth trap. The Speaker's decision under the Tenth Schedule does have finality — but not absolute finality in all circumstances. Kihoto Hollohan created limited judicial review grounds (mala fides, perversity, natural justice). Students who know 'Speaker's decisions are final' without the Kihoto qualification will accept Statement 3 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Not all areas traditionally thought to be beyond judicial review actually are — the Indian Constitution and jurisprudence reveal a nuanced map.

| Statement | Verdict |
|---|---|
| 1. Article 105(2) — absolute bar on reviewing parliamentary speech | Correct |
| 2. Article 74(2) — absolute bar on reviewing ministerial advice | Correct |
| 3. Tenth Schedule — Speaker's order conclusively immune in all circumstances | Incorrect |
| 4. Post-44th Amendment Emergency procedural requirements are justiciable | Correct |

Three statements are correct.

**Value Addition:**
• The equivalent of Article 74(2) for States is Article 163(3) — advice by State Council of Ministers to Governor is also judicially non-reviewable.
• Article 105(2) immunity extends to witnesses summoned to give evidence before Parliamentary committees within Parliament.
• Nabam Rebia (2016) added another dimension: a Speaker with a pending removal notice cannot adjudicate disqualification petitions — further limiting the Speaker's unchecked power.

Zachillhu (1992) में सर्वोच्च न्यायालय ने कहा कि पैरा 7 (जो स्पीकर के निर्णयों की सभी न्यायिक समीक्षा को रोकता था) मूलभूत संरचना का उल्लंघन करता है। स्पीकर के आदेशों की समीक्षा माला फाइड्स, विकृति, या प्राकृतिक न्याय के उल्लंघन के आधार पर की जा सकती है।

statement_analysis.statement: अनुच्छेद 352 के तहत राष्ट्रीय आपातकाल की राष्ट्रपति घोषणा 44वें संवैधानिक संशोधन द्वारा लागू अनिवार्य प्रक्रियात्मक आवश्यकताओं का पालन न किए जाने पर न्यायिक रूप से समीक्षा योग्य है।

solution.concept_anchor: R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala — severability test and legislative intent
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) 'the court determines whether the legislature would have enacted only the valid part independently of the invalid part' is the correct formulation of the severability test and appears in option (a) but is attributed to the wrong case. Students who know the test but not the case name will select (a) if the case name is wrong.
elimination_logic: The question asks for the case that established the severability doctrine's governing test in India.

The Chamarbaugwala case (1957) — R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala v. Union of India — established the test: would Parliament have enacted the valid portion alone, absent the invalid portion? Legislative intent is central.
Eliminate Keshavan Madhava Menon — this 1951 case dealt with Article 13(1) and eclipse, not severability.
Eliminate A.K. Gopalan — this 1950 case dealt with preventive detention and Articles 19/21, not severability.
R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala v. Union of India (1957) is the foundational severability case — option (c) is correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap pairs the correct legal test (legislative intent — would the legislature have enacted the valid part alone?) with an incorrect case name in option (a), and places the correct case name (Chamarbaugwala) with the correct test in option (c). A student who has memorised the test but not the case will need to identify which case-test combination is correctly matched.
solution.final_explanation:
The Doctrine of Severability allows courts to preserve the constitutional portions of a statute when only a part is invalid.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The test described is correct — legislative intent is the key — but the Keshavan Madhava Menon case dealt with the transitional provisions of the Constitution and Article 13(1), not with severability.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: A.K. Gopalan v. State of India (1950) was a landmark preventive detention case involving Articles 19 and 21, unrelated to the severability doctrine.
• Option (c) — Correct: R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala v. Union of India (1957) is the foundational Indian authority on severability. The Court held that if a portion of a statute is unconstitutional, the court must ask: would the legislature have enacted the valid portion alone? If yes, only the invalid portion is struck down. Legislative intent — not mechanical linguistic division — is the controlling test.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Golaknath case dealt with whether constitutional amendments are 'law' under Article 13 and introduced prospective overruling; it is not a severability authority.

**Value Addition:**
• The Blue Pencil rule (companion to severability) allows courts to strike out offensive words but not to rewrite, add, or reconstruct provisions.
• If the valid and invalid parts are so intertwined that they cannot be separated without changing the substance of the Act, the entire law is struck down.
• Severability applies to post-constitutional laws; pre-constitutional laws in the same situation would be governed by the Eclipse doctrine.

formatted_presentation.display_text:
The test for applying the Doctrine of Severability in Indian constitutional law was authoritatively laid down in ________, which held that a court must determine whether the legislature would have enacted the valid part of a statute independently of the invalid part, making legislative intent the central inquiry.

(a) Keshavan Madhava Menon v. State of Bombay (1951)
(b) A.K. Gopalan v. State of India (1950)
(c) R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala v. Union of India (1957)
(d) Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967)

solution.strong_distractor: a — विकल्प (a) 'अदालत यह निर्धारित करती है कि क्या विधायिका केवल मान्य भाग को अवैध भाग से स्वतंत्र रूप से लागू करती' यह पृथक्करण परीक्षण का सही सूत्रीकरण है और विकल्प (a) में है लेकिन गलत मामले के साथ जोड़ा गया है। जो छात्र परीक्षण जानते हैं लेकिन मामले का नाम नहीं जानते, वे (a) चुनेंगे यदि मामला नाम गलत हो।
elimination_logic: प्रश्न उस मामले के लिए है जिसने भारत में पृथक्करण सिद्धांत के शासन परीक्षण की स्थापना की।
चमारबाउगवाला मामला (1957) — R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala बनाम भारत संघ — ने परीक्षण स्थापित किया: क्या संसद ने केवल मान्य भाग को लागू किया होता, यदि अवैध भाग न होता? विधायी इरादा केंद्रीय है।
केशवन माधव मेनन को हटा दें — यह 1951 का मामला अनुच्छेद 13(1) और ग्रहण (eclipse) से संबंधित था, पृथक्करण से नहीं।
ए.के. गोपालन को हटा दें — यह 1950 का मामला निवारक हिरासत और अनुच्छेद 19/21 से संबंधित था, पृथक्करण से नहीं।
R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala बनाम भारत संघ (1957) मौलिक पृथक्करण मामला है — विकल्प (c) सही है।
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: इकाई-स्थानांतरण जाल में सही कानूनी परीक्षण (विधायी इरादा — क्या विधायिका केवल मान्य भाग को लागू करती?) को विकल्प (a) में गलत मामले के नाम के साथ जोड़ा गया है, और सही मामले का नाम (चमारबाउगवाला) सही परीक्षण के साथ विकल्प (c) में रखा गया है। जो छात्र परीक्षण याद रखते हैं लेकिन मामले का नाम नहीं जानते, उन्हें सही मामले-टेस्ट संयोजन पहचानना होगा।
solution.final_explanation:
पृथक्करण सिद्धांत अदालतों को यह अनुमति देता है कि जब किसी अधिनियम का केवल एक भाग अवैध हो तो संवैधानिक भागों को संरक्षित किया जाए।

• विकल्प (a) — गलत: वर्णित परीक्षण सही है — विधायी इरादा मुख्य है — लेकिन केशवन माधव मेनन मामला संविधान के संक्रमणकालीन प्रावधानों और अनुच्छेद 13(1) से संबंधित था, पृथक्करण से नहीं।
• विकल्प (b) — गलत: ए.के. गोपालन बनाम भारत राज्य (1950) एक महत्वपूर्ण निवारक हिरासत मामला था जिसमें अनुच्छेद 19 और 21 शामिल थे, पृथक्करण सिद्धांत से असंबंधित।
• विकल्प (c) — सही: R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala बनाम भारत संघ (1957) भारत में पृथक्करण पर मौलिक प्राधिकरण है। अदालत ने कहा कि यदि अधिनियम का कोई भाग असंवैधानिक है, तो अदालत को यह पूछना चाहिए: क्या विधायिका केवल मान्य भाग को लागू करती? यदि हाँ, तो केवल अवैध भाग को रद्द किया जाता है। विधायी इरादा — न कि यांत्रिक भाषाई विभाजन — नियंत्रण परीक्षण है।
• विकल्प (d) — गलत: गोलकनाथ मामला इस बात से संबंधित था कि क्या संवैधानिक संशोधन अनुच्छेद 13 के तहत 'कानून' हैं और इसने प्रत्याशित निराकरण (prospective overruling) पेश किया; यह पृथक्करण प्राधिकरण नहीं है।

**मूल्य संवर्धन:**
• ब्लू पेंसिल नियम (पृथक्करण का साथी) अदालतों को आपत्तिजनक शब्दों को हटाने की अनुमति देता है लेकिन प्रावधानों को पुनः लिखने, जोड़ने या पुनर्निर्माण करने की अनुमति नहीं देता।
• यदि मान्य और अवैध भाग इतने अंतर्संबंधित हैं कि उन्हें अधिनियम की सामग्री बदले बिना अलग नहीं किया जा सकता, तो पूरा कानून रद्द कर दिया जाता है।
• पृथक्करण संवैधानिक बाद के कानूनों पर लागू होता है; संवैधानिक पूर्व के कानूनों के लिए इसी स्थिति में ग्रहण सिद्धांत लागू होगा।

solution.concept_anchor: Article 31C post-Minerva Mills — limited to Articles 39(b) and 39(c) only
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is the strong distractor because students who know Minerva Mills (1980) struck down the extension of Article 31C and that the balance between Part III and Part IV is a Basic Structure element may assume R (correctly about Minerva Mills) explains A (correctly about Article 31C's current scope), without checking whether A is itself stated accurately.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — A states: 'Post-Minerva Mills, Article 31C protection extends to laws implementing ANY Directive Principle of State Policy.' This is precisely what Minerva Mills struck down. Post-Minerva Mills, Article 31C protection extends only to Articles 39(b) and 39(c), NOT to all DPSPs. A is INCORRECT.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — R states: 'Minerva Mills (1980) held that the balance between Fundamental Rights (Part III) and Directive Principles (Part IV) is itself an element of the Basic Structure.' This is accurate — Minerva Mills held that destroying this balance would violate the Basic Structure. R is correct.
Step 3: Causal link is irrelevant since A is incorrect.
A is incorrect, R is correct — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Assertion (A) restates the 42nd Amendment's expansion of Article 31C (which extended it to all DPSPs) as if this expansion is the current law. Minerva Mills (1980) specifically struck down this extension. Students who confuse what Parliament attempted (via the 42nd Amendment) with what the courts allowed (only 39(b) and 39(c)) will accept A as correct and gravitate toward options (a) or (b). The trap tests whether the student knows not just that Minerva Mills is important, but what precisely it did and did not allow.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 31C was inserted by the 25th Constitutional Amendment (1971) to shield laws implementing Articles 39(b) and 39(c) from challenges under Articles 14 and 19. The 42nd Amendment (1976) extended this protection to all Directive Principles — giving complete legislative supremacy to Parliament on any DPSP. Minerva Mills (1980) struck down this blanket extension.

**Assertion (A):** Incorrect — A states that post-Minerva Mills, Article 31C extends to laws implementing ANY Directive Principle. This is precisely the opposite of what Minerva Mills held. Post-Minerva Mills, Article 31C protection is restored to its original scope: only laws specifically implementing Articles 39(b) (equitable distribution of material resources) and 39(c) (prevention of concentration of wealth and means of production) enjoy immunity from Articles 14 and 19 challenges.

**Reason (R):** Correct — Minerva Mills (1980) held that the harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is itself a Basic Structure element. A constitutional amendment that wholly subordinates Part III to Part IV destroys this balance and is invalid.

A is incorrect; R is correct — option (d).

**Value Addition:**
• The 42nd Amendment (1976) also made Article 368 immune from judicial challenge — this too was struck down in Minerva Mills.
• Even within Articles 39(b) and 39(c), the Supreme Court in Kesavananda Bharati curtailed Article 31C by requiring that a law genuinely have the declared DPSP object.
• The Kerala Education Bill case (1958) and Unni Krishnan v. State of AP (1993) are also part of the FR–DPSP harmonisation jurisprudence.

formatted_presentation.display_text:
Assertion (A): Post-Minerva Mills, Article 31C of the Constitution provides immunity from challenge under Articles 14 and 19 to laws enacted by Parliament or State Legislatures for giving effect to any of the Directive Principles of State Policy contained in Part IV of the Constitution.

Reason (R): The Supreme Court in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) held that the harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights in Part III and Directive Principles in Part IV constitutes an element of the Basic Structure of the Constitution and cannot be destroyed by a constitutional amendment.

(a) Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A
(b) Both A and R are correct, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

अनुच्छेद 31C को 25वें संविधान संशोधन (1971) द्वारा जोड़ा गया था ताकि अनुच्छेद 39(b) और 39(c) को लागू करने वाले कानूनों को अनुच्छेद 14 और 19 के तहत चुनौतियों से सुरक्षा मिल सके। 42वें संशोधन (1976) ने इस संरक्षण को सभी निर्देशात्मक सिद्धांतों तक बढ़ा दिया — जिससे संसद को किसी भी DPSP पर पूर्ण विधायी सर्वोच्चता मिल गई। Minerva Mills (1980) ने इस समग्र विस्तार को खारिज कर दिया।

**कथन (A):** गलत — A कहता है कि Minerva Mills के बाद अनुच्छेद 31C किसी भी निर्देशात्मक सिद्धांत को लागू करने वाले कानूनों तक विस्तृत है। यह बिल्कुल विपरीत है जो Minerva Mills ने कहा। Minerva Mills के बाद, अनुच्छेद 31C का संरक्षण अपने मूल दायरे में पुनः स्थापित हो गया है: केवल वे कानून जो विशेष रूप से अनुच्छेद 39(b) (सामग्री संसाधनों का न्यायसंगत वितरण) और 39(c) (धन और उत्पादन के साधनों के संकेंद्रण की रोकथाम) को लागू करते हैं, अनुच्छेद 14 और 19 की चुनौतियों से मुक्त हैं।

**कारण (R):** सही — Minerva Mills (1980) ने कहा कि मौलिक अधिकार और निर्देशात्मक सिद्धांतों के बीच सामंजस्य और संतुलन स्वयं मौलिक संरचना का एक तत्व है। एक ऐसा संवैधानिक संशोधन जो पूरी तरह से भाग III को भाग IV के अधीन कर देता है, इस संतुलन को नष्ट करता है और अमान्य है।

A गलत है; R सही है — विकल्प (d)।

**मूल्य संवर्धन:**
• 42वें संशोधन (1976) ने अनुच्छेद 368 को भी न्यायिक चुनौती से मुक्त कर दिया था — इसे भी Minerva Mills में खारिज कर दिया गया।
• अनुच्छेद 39(b) और 39(c) के भीतर भी, सुप्रीम कोर्ट ने केसवनंद भारती मामले में अनुच्छेद 31C को सीमित किया कि कानून का वास्तविक DPSP उद्देश्य होना चाहिए।
• केरल एजुकेशन बिल मामला (1958) और उन्नी कृष्णन बनाम आंध्र प्रदेश राज्य (1993) भी मौलिक अधिकार–निर्देशात्मक सिद्धांत सामंजस्य न्यायशास्त्र का हिस्सा हैं।

solution.concept_anchor: M. Nagaraj — triple test for SC/ST promotion reservations

statement_analysis.statement: In M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006), the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of Articles 16(4A) and 16(4B) but required States to demonstrate three conditions before extending reservation in promotions to SCs and STs: backwardness of the community, inadequate representation in the cadre, and no adverse effect on administrative efficiency.
statement_analysis.reason: M. Nagaraj (2006) upheld the 77th, 81st, 82nd, and 85th Constitutional Amendments but held that States must satisfy a triple-test before providing reservation in promotions — demonstrating community backwardness, inadequate representation, and preservation of overall administrative efficiency as required by Article 335.

statement_analysis.statement: Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta (2018) overruled M. Nagaraj in its entirety and held that States need not demonstrate any condition before providing reservation in promotions for SCs and STs.
statement_analysis.reason: Jarnail Singh (2018) only overruled the specific requirement of collecting quantifiable data to demonstrate the backwardness of SCs/STs — since their backwardness is constitutionally presumed. It retained the requirements of demonstrating inadequate representation and maintaining administrative efficiency. It did not overrule M. Nagaraj entirely.

statement_analysis.statement: The 50% ceiling on reservations, including reservation in promotions, applies to SCs and STs just as it applies to OBCs.
statement_analysis.reason: M. Nagaraj (2006) confirmed that the 50% ceiling from Indra Sawhney (1992) applies to all reservations including those in promotions for SCs and STs — it is not a ceiling only for OBC reservations.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) includes Statement 2, which sounds plausible because Jarnail Singh (2018) is commonly described as having 'overruled Nagaraj' — students who know this headline but not the precise scope of the overruling will mark Statement 2 as correct and choose an option that includes it.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: M. Nagaraj (2006) — triple-test: backwardness, inadequate representation, administrative efficiency. This is the correct holding. Statement 1 is correct.

Statement 2: Jarnail Singh (2018) overruled only the quantifiable data requirement for SC/ST backwardness — it did NOT overrule M. Nagaraj in its entirety. Inadequate representation and administrative efficiency requirements remain. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 3: The 50% ceiling applies universally to all reservations including promotions — confirmed in M. Nagaraj. Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct; Statement 2 incorrect — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a classic partial-truth construction: Jarnail Singh (2018) did overrule a specific part of M. Nagaraj — the quantifiable data requirement for SC/ST backwardness. But students who have heard the shorthand 'Jarnail Singh overruled Nagaraj' without reading the nuance will treat Statement 2 as fully correct. The precise holding is a partial overruling — and the two retained conditions (inadequate representation and administrative efficiency) make Statement 2's claim of complete overruling false.
solution.final_explanation:
M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006) is the constitutional gateway case for reservation in promotions for SCs and STs.

• Statement 1 — Correct: A five-judge bench in Nagaraj upheld the 77th Constitutional Amendment inserting Article 16(4A) (reservation in promotions for SCs/STs) and Article 16(4B) (carry-forward). However, the Court imposed a triple precondition on States: they must demonstrate (i) the community's backwardness; (ii) inadequate representation in the promoted cadre; and (iii) overall administrative efficiency is maintained as required by Article 335.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The characterisation 'overruled M. Nagaraj in its entirety' is wrong. Jarnail Singh (2018) overruled only the requirement of collecting quantifiable data to establish SC/ST backwardness — reasoning that constitutional recognition of SC/ST backwardness in Article 341 and 342 makes fresh data-collection unnecessary. But the other two requirements — inadequate representation and administrative efficiency — were affirmed and retained.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The 50% ceiling from Indra Sawhney (1992) is applied to all reservations, including those in promotions. M. Nagaraj confirmed this ceiling applies to SC/ST promotion reservations as well.

**Value Addition:**
• Article 335 specifically requires that the claims of SCs/STs be taken into account consistently with the maintenance of efficiency of administration — it is a constitutional constraint on the degree of promotional reservation.
• The 85th Constitutional Amendment added the concept of 'consequential seniority' for SC/ST promotion reservations — this too was upheld in Nagaraj.
• The question of whether creamy layer should apply to SCs in the context of promotions remains constitutionally open post-Jarnail Singh.

• कथन 1 — सही: Nagaraj की पांच-न्यायाधीश पीठ ने 77वें संवैधानिक संशोधन को बनाए रखा जिसमें अनुच्छेद 16(4A) (एससी/एसटी के लिए पदोन्नति में आरक्षण) और अनुच्छेद 16(4B) (कैरी-फॉरवर्ड) शामिल हैं। हालांकि, न्यायालय ने राज्यों पर तीन पूर्व-शर्तें लगाईं: (i) समुदाय की पिछड़ापन; (ii) पदोन्नति वाले वर्ग में अपर्याप्त प्रतिनिधित्व; और (iii) अनुच्छेद 335 के अनुसार समग्र प्रशासनिक दक्षता का संरक्षण।
• कथन 2 — गलत: 'M. Nagaraj को पूरी तरह रद्द कर दिया' का वर्णन गलत है। Jarnail Singh (2018) ने केवल एससी/एसटी पिछड़ापन सिद्ध करने के लिए मात्रात्मक डेटा की आवश्यकता को रद्द किया — यह तर्क देते हुए कि अनुच्छेद 341 और 342 में एससी/एसटी पिछड़ापन संवैधानिक रूप से मान्य है, इसलिए नया डेटा संग्रह आवश्यक नहीं। लेकिन अन्य दो शर्तें — अपर्याप्त प्रतिनिधित्व और प्रशासनिक दक्षता — बनाए रखी गईं।
• कथन 3 — सही: इंद्रा साहनी (1992) से 50% की सीमा सभी आरक्षणों पर लागू होती है, जिसमें पदोन्नति में आरक्षण भी शामिल है। M. Nagaraj ने इस सीमा को एससी/एसटी पदोन्नति आरक्षण पर भी लागू किया।

**मूल्य संवर्धन:**
• अनुच्छेद 335 विशेष रूप से यह आवश्यक करता है कि एससी/एसटी के दावे प्रशासन की दक्षता बनाए रखते हुए ध्यान में लिए जाएं — यह पदोन्नति आरक्षण की सीमा पर संवैधानिक प्रतिबंध है।
• 85वें संवैधानिक संशोधन ने एससी/एसटी पदोन्नति आरक्षण के लिए 'परिणामी वरिष्ठता' की अवधारणा जोड़ी — इसे भी Nagaraj में बनाए रखा गया।
• पदोन्नति के संदर्भ में एससी के लिए क्रीमी लेयर लागू होनी चाहिए या नहीं, यह प्रश्न Jarnail Singh के बाद संवैधानिक रूप से खुला है।

solution.concept_anchor: PIL limits — what courts cannot do through judicial activism
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) 'Issuing guidelines in the absence of legislation to protect a constitutional right' is a strong distractor because students who know courts have done this (Vishaka guidelines) but also know courts are not supposed to 'legislate' may incorrectly classify this as an instance of overreach rather than recognised activism.
elimination_logic: Identify which three items belong to recognised legitimate judicial review/activism and which one is judicial overreach beyond acceptable limits.
Option (a) — Treating a letter from a prison inmate as a writ petition: Epistolary jurisdiction — recognised legitimate expansion of Article 32/226. Belongs.
Option (b) — Issuing guidelines in absence of legislation to protect a constitutional right: Vishaka-type activism — recognised as legitimate judicial gap-filling. Belongs.

Option (c) — Directing Parliament to enact a specific law within a time-bound deadline: This crosses the constitutional line — separation of powers prohibits courts from directing the legislature on what law to enact. Courts may indicate a need for legislation but cannot compel Parliament by injunction.

Option (d) — Monitoring implementation of an environment protection order through a continuing mandamus: Recognised judicial activism tool — courts routinely issue continuing mandamus in environment and infrastructure cases. Belongs.
Option (c) is the odd one out — the one that courts CANNOT do. Select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges judicial activism (legitimate gap-filling) with judicial overreach (directing Parliament to legislate). Students who are critical of 'judicial overreach' may also classify option (b) — Vishaka-type guideline issuance — as overreach. The precise constitutional principle is that courts can fill a legislative vacuum through guidelines but cannot direct Parliament as a legislature to enact a particular law. Option (c) is the clear overreach; option (b) is accepted activism.
solution.final_explanation:
The boundary between judicial activism and judicial overreach is one of the most nuanced areas tested in judicial review questions.

• Option (a) — Belongs to legitimate judicial review: Epistolary jurisdiction (treating a letter as a writ petition) was recognised in Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration — a constitutional innovation allowing disadvantaged persons without legal resources to access courts.
• Option (b) — Belongs to legitimate judicial review: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) established that in the absence of legislation, courts may issue binding guidelines as a temporary measure to protect constitutional rights. This is judicial gap-filling — recognised by the Court itself as appropriate under Articles 32 and 141.
• Option (c) — The odd one out: Courts cannot direct Parliament to pass a specific law within a time-bound deadline. This would violate the separation of powers — itself a Basic Structure element. Courts may recommend legislation or indicate its absence, but cannot compel Parliament in the exercise of its legislative function.
• Option (d) — Belongs to legitimate judicial review: Continuing mandamus — monitoring compliance with court orders — is a recognised tool used in cases like Vineet Narain v. Union of India and numerous environmental protection cases.

**Value Addition:**
• The Supreme Court distinguished between 'judicial activism' and 'judicial overreach' in Divisional Manager, Aravali Golf Club v. Chander Hass (2008) — cautioning against overreach into executive and legislative domains.
• A court can ask Parliament to 'consider' enacting a law — it cannot set a deadline or dictate content.
• Continuing mandamus is most prominent in environmental cases, prison reform cases, and right to food cases.

concepts_used: Public Interest Litigation (PIL) as an Expanded Form of Judicial Review
Judicial Review vs. Judicial Activism vs. Judicial Overreach: Conceptual Distinctions

solution.concept_anchor: PIL limits — what courts cannot do through judicial activism
solution.strong_distractor: b — विकल्प (b) 'संसदीय विधायिका के अभाव में संवैधानिक अधिकार की रक्षा के लिए दिशानिर्देश जारी करना' एक मजबूत भ्रम पैदा करने वाला विकल्प है क्योंकि छात्र जानते हैं कि न्यायालयों ने ऐसा किया है (विशाखा दिशानिर्देश) लेकिन साथ ही जानते हैं कि न्यायालयों को 'विधायिका' नहीं करनी चाहिए, अतः वे इसे ओवररीच के बजाय मान्यता प्राप्त सक्रियता के रूप में गलत वर्गीकृत कर सकते हैं।
elimination_logic: पहचानिए कि कौन से तीन आइटम मान्यता प्राप्त वैध न्यायिक समीक्षा/सक्रियता के अंतर्गत आते हैं और कौन सा एक न्यायिक ओवररीच है जो स्वीकार्य सीमाओं से परे है।
विकल्प (a) — एक कैदी द्वारा लिखा गया पत्र एक रिट याचिका के रूप में मानना: पत्राचार अधिकार क्षेत्र — अनुच्छेद 32/226 का मान्यता प्राप्त वैध विस्तार। शामिल है।
विकल्प (b) — संसदीय विधायिका के अभाव में संवैधानिक अधिकार की रक्षा के लिए दिशानिर्देश जारी करना: विशाखा प्रकार की सक्रियता — न्यायिक अंतराल पूर्ति के रूप में मान्यता प्राप्त वैधता। शामिल है।

विकल्प (c) — संसद को एक विशिष्ट कानून निर्धारित समय सीमा के भीतर बनाने का निर्देश देना: यह संवैधानिक सीमा को पार करता है — शक्तियों के पृथक्करण के कारण न्यायालय विधायिका को यह निर्देश नहीं दे सकते कि कौन सा कानून बनाना है। न्यायालय कानून की आवश्यकता संकेतित कर सकते हैं लेकिन संसद को बाध्य नहीं कर सकते।

विकल्प (d) — पर्यावरण संरक्षण आदेश के पालन की निगरानी के लिए निरंतर मंडामस जारी करना: मान्यता प्राप्त न्यायिक सक्रियता उपकरण — न्यायालय पर्यावरण और अवसंरचना मामलों में नियमित रूप से निरंतर मंडामस जारी करते हैं। शामिल है।
विकल्प (c) अलग है — वह कार्य जो न्यायालय नहीं कर सकते। विकल्प (c) चुनें।
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: मिश्रण जाल न्यायिक सक्रियता (वैध अंतराल पूर्ति) को न्यायिक ओवररीच (संसद को विधायिका करने का निर्देश देना) के साथ मिला देता है। जो छात्र 'न्यायिक ओवररीच' के आलोचक हैं, वे विकल्प (b) — विशाखा प्रकार के दिशानिर्देश जारी करने — को भी ओवररीच मान सकते हैं। सटीक संवैधानिक सिद्धांत यह है कि न्यायालय विधायी शून्यता को दिशानिर्देशों के माध्यम से भर सकते हैं लेकिन संसद को किसी विशेष कानून को पारित करने का निर्देश नहीं दे सकते। विकल्प (c) स्पष्ट ओवररीच है; विकल्प (b) स्वीकार्य सक्रियता है।
solution.final_explanation:
न्यायिक सक्रियता और न्यायिक ओवररीच के बीच की सीमा न्यायिक समीक्षा प्रश्नों में सबसे सूक्ष्म क्षेत्रों में से एक है।

• विकल्प (a) — वैध न्यायिक समीक्षा के अंतर्गत आता है: पत्राचार अधिकार क्षेत्र (एक पत्र को रिट याचिका मानना) सनिल बत्रा बनाम दिल्ली प्रशासन में मान्यता प्राप्त — एक संवैधानिक नवाचार जो कानूनी संसाधनहीन वंचित व्यक्तियों को न्यायालयों तक पहुँच प्रदान करता है।
• विकल्प (b) — वैध न्यायिक समीक्षा के अंतर्गत आता है: विशाखा बनाम राजस्थान राज्य (1997) में स्थापित कि विधायिका के अभाव में न्यायालय संवैधानिक अधिकारों की रक्षा के लिए बाध्यकारी दिशानिर्देश जारी कर सकते हैं। यह न्यायिक अंतराल पूर्ति है — जिसे न्यायालय ने अनुच्छेद 32 और 141 के तहत उपयुक्त माना है।
• विकल्प (c) — अलग विकल्प: न्यायालय संसद को किसी विशिष्ट कानून को समयबद्ध सीमा के भीतर पारित करने का निर्देश नहीं दे सकते। यह शक्तियों के पृथक्करण का उल्लंघन होगा — जो कि मौलिक संरचना का तत्व है। न्यायालय विधायिका की अनुपस्थिति या आवश्यकता की ओर संकेत कर सकते हैं, लेकिन संसद को बाध्य नहीं कर सकते।
• विकल्प (d) — वैध न्यायिक समीक्षा के अंतर्गत आता है: निरंतर मंडामस — न्यायालय आदेशों के पालन की निगरानी — जैसे विनीत नरैन बनाम भारत संघ और अनेक पर्यावरण संरक्षण मामलों में उपयोग किया जाता है।

**मूल्य संवर्धन:**
• सुप्रीम कोर्ट ने डिविजनल मैनेजर, अरावली गोल्फ क्लब बनाम चंदर हस (2008) में 'न्यायिक सक्रियता' और 'न्यायिक ओवररीच' के बीच अंतर स्पष्ट किया — कार्यकारी और विधायी क्षेत्रों में ओवररीच से सावधानी बरतने की चेतावनी दी।
• न्यायालय संसद से कानून बनाने पर 'विचार' करने को कह सकते हैं — वे समय सीमा निर्धारित या सामग्री निर्धारित नहीं कर सकते।
• निरंतर मंडामस पर्यावरण, जेल सुधार और भोजन के अधिकार जैसे मामलों में सबसे अधिक प्रचलित है।

solution.concept_anchor: S.R. Bommai — Article 356 judicial review and floor test
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students who know S.R. Bommai is the landmark Article 356 case may not know the precise holding — that courts can restore a dissolved Assembly — and may choose an option that describes a narrower holding.
elimination_logic: Identify which case-holding pair about judicial review of Emergency provisions is correctly matched.

S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994): 9-judge bench held that proclamation of President's Rule under Article 356 is subject to full judicial review; courts can restore a dissolved State Legislative Assembly; the floor test is the proper measure of majority.

Eliminate option (b): It pairs Bommai with a holding that 'courts can only examine procedural compliance, not the substantive ground' — this understates Bommai; courts can review the substantive satisfaction of the President.

Eliminate option (c): It pairs the 44th Amendment with the holding that 'Article 356 proclamations are entirely non-justiciable' — this was the pre-44th Amendment and pre-Bommai position, not the current law.
Eliminate option (d): It pairs State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977) with a holding about Article 356 — but that case was about Article 352 (National Emergency), not Article 356.
Option (a) correctly pairs S.R. Bommai (1994) with the holding that courts can review the proclamation of President's Rule and can restore a dissolved Assembly — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap here pairs the correct holding (full judicial review of Article 356 proclamations, restoration of Assembly) with S.R. Bommai in option (a), and creates plausible wrong pairings by attributing partial or inverted Bommai holdings to other cases. Students who know Bommai is the 'Article 356 case' but have not internalised the precise holding (especially the Assembly restoration power) may be uncertain about option (a) vs. option (b).
solution.final_explanation:
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) is the definitive constitutional authority on Article 356 and its reviewability.

• Option (a) — Correctly matched: Bommai (1994), decided by a nine-judge bench, held that proclamations under Article 356 are subject to full judicial review on both procedural and substantive grounds. The floor test — a vote of confidence in the Legislative Assembly — is the constitutionally proper measure of a government's majority. Significantly, the Court held that if a proclamation is found unconstitutional, courts can restore the dissolved Assembly.
• Option (b) — Incorrectly matched: Bommai does not limit review to procedural compliance. It allows courts to examine whether the President was satisfied on relevant and adequate material — a substantive review.
• Option (c) — Incorrectly matched: The 44th Amendment (1978) reformed the grounds for National Emergency (Article 352), not Article 356. It did not render Article 356 proclamations non-justiciable — Bommai subsequently confirmed full reviewability.
• Option (d) — Incorrectly matched: State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977) dealt with the justiciability of proclamations under Article 352 (National Emergency), holding them non-justiciable pre-44th Amendment. It did not address Article 356.

**Value Addition:**
• Bommai identified secularism and federalism as Basic Structure elements — governments that subvert secularism cannot claim Article 356 protection.
• The floor test principle from Bommai has been applied repeatedly in state political crises — most recently in Maharashtra (2019) and Rajasthan (2020).
• Bommai also held that President's Rule should be used as a last resort, not the first response to political instability.

solution.final_explanation:
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) अनुच्छेद 356 और उसकी समीक्षा पर निर्णायक संवैधानिक प्राधिकरण है।

• विकल्प (a) — सही मेल: Bommai (1994), नौ-न्यायाधीशों की पीठ द्वारा निर्णयित, ने कहा कि अनुच्छेद 356 के तहत घोषणाएँ प्रक्रियात्मक और मूलभूत दोनों आधारों पर पूर्ण न्यायिक समीक्षा के अधीन हैं। फ्लोर टेस्ट — विधायी सभा में विश्वास मत — सरकार के बहुमत का संवैधानिक रूप से उचित मापदंड है। महत्वपूर्ण रूप से, न्यायालय ने कहा कि यदि घोषणा असंवैधानिक पाई जाती है, तो न्यायालय भंग की गई विधानसभा को पुनर्स्थापित कर सकते हैं।
• विकल्प (b) — गलत मेल: Bommai समीक्षा को केवल प्रक्रियात्मक अनुपालन तक सीमित नहीं करता। यह न्यायालयों को यह जांचने की अनुमति देता है कि क्या राष्ट्रपति संबंधित और पर्याप्त सामग्री पर संतुष्ट थे — एक मूलभूत समीक्षा।
• विकल्प (c) — गलत मेल: 44वां संशोधन (1978) राष्ट्रीय आपातकाल (अनुच्छेद 352) के आधारों में सुधार लाया, न कि अनुच्छेद 356 में। इसने अनुच्छेद 356 की घोषणाओं को न्यायिक समीक्षा से बाहर नहीं किया — Bommai ने बाद में पूर्ण समीक्षा की पुष्टि की।
• विकल्प (d) — गलत मेल: राजस्थान राज्य बनाम भारत संघ (1977) ने अनुच्छेद 352 (राष्ट्रीय आपातकाल) के तहत घोषणाओं की न्यायिक समीक्षा से बाहर होने का निर्णय दिया, जो 44वें संशोधन से पहले था। इसने अनुच्छेद 356 को संबोधित नहीं किया।

**मूल्य संवर्धन:**
• Bommai ने धर्मनिरपेक्षता और संघवाद को मूलभूत संरचना के तत्व के रूप में पहचाना — जो सरकारें धर्मनिरपेक्षता को कमजोर करती हैं, वे अनुच्छेद 356 की सुरक्षा का दावा नहीं कर सकतीं।
• Bommai का फ्लोर टेस्ट सिद्धांत राज्य राजनीतिक संकटों में बार-बार लागू हुआ है — हाल ही में महाराष्ट्र (2019) और राजस्थान (2020) में।
• Bommai ने यह भी कहा कि राष्ट्रपति शासन का उपयोग राजनीतिक अस्थिरता के पहले उपाय के रूप में नहीं, बल्कि अंतिम उपाय के रूप में किया जाना चाहिए।

solution.concept_anchor: Maneka Gandhi — Articles 14, 19, 21 read together, reasonableness of procedure

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 1: In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), the Supreme Court held that the word 'procedure' in Article 21 must be right, just, and fair — not arbitrary, fanciful, or oppressive — effectively reading substantive reasonableness into a provision that, by its text, only required procedural compliance.
statement_analysis.reason: Maneka Gandhi (1978) rejected the A.K. Gopalan approach that read each fundamental right in isolation. The Court held that Articles 14, 19, and 21 must be read together, and that any procedure depriving a person of life or liberty must satisfy the requirements of reasonableness under Article 14 and must not be unreasonably restrictive of rights under Article 19.

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 2: The Constituent Assembly deliberately replaced the phrase 'due process of law' with 'procedure established by law' in Article 21 because Dr. Ambedkar and others feared that 'due process' would give courts excessively wide power to strike down social welfare legislation — confirming that India intended a purely procedural Article 21 with no substantive element.
statement_analysis.reason: The second part of Statement 2 is incorrect. While the Constituent Assembly did deliberately replace 'due process of law' with 'procedure established by law,' this historical choice does not confirm that Article 21 was intended to be permanently purely procedural. Maneka Gandhi (1978) evolved Article 21 jurisprudence to read in substantive elements through a holistic reading with Articles 14 and 19 — this judicial evolution is constitutionally recognised and not negated by the original drafting history.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) 'Both statements correct' is a strong distractor because Statement 2's first clause (Constituent Assembly replaced 'due process' with 'procedure established by law') is factually accurate, and students reading quickly may not catch that the second clause ('confirming permanently purely procedural') is made false by the Maneka Gandhi evolution.
elimination_logic: Test Statement 1: Maneka Gandhi (1978) — 'procedure' must be right, just, fair; Articles 14, 19, 21 read together; substantive reasonableness read into Article 21. Statement 1 is correct.

Test Statement 2: First clause — Constituent Assembly replaced 'due process' with 'procedure established by law' — correct historical fact. Second clause — 'confirming that India intended a permanently purely procedural Article 21 with no substantive element' — this is made false by Maneka Gandhi. Statement 2's conclusion does not follow from the premise. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses a reversed-causation structure: the premise (Constituent Assembly replaced 'due process') is true, but the conclusion drawn from it (India 'confirmed' purely procedural Article 21 permanently) does not follow and is negated by post-1978 judicial interpretation. A student who verifies only the premise and accepts the conclusion without question will mark Statement 2 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
The history and evolution of Article 21 is one of the most tested threads in constitutional law.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) marks the watershed in Article 21 interpretation. The Supreme Court overruled the narrow A.K. Gopalan approach (that each fundamental right was a separate watertight compartment) and held that Articles 14, 19, and 21 must be read as a composite framework. Any procedure that takes away life or liberty must be fair, just, and reasonable — not a mere formality. This imported substantive due process elements into what the text presented as a purely procedural guarantee.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The first clause is historically accurate — the Constituent Assembly consciously used 'procedure established by law' to avoid US-style substantive due process review of economic/social legislation. However, Statement 2's conclusion — that this choice 'confirmed a permanently purely procedural Article 21' — is false. Maneka Gandhi demonstrated that judicial interpretation can evolve beyond the original textual choice, and this evolution is constitutionally legitimate.

**Value Addition:**
• Post-Maneka Gandhi, the right to life under Article 21 has been expanded to include the right to livelihood (Olga Tellis, 1985), right to health, right to education (before Article 21A was inserted), and right to privacy (Puttaswamy, 2017).
• A.K. Gopalan v. State of India (1950) was the pre-Maneka authority — held each FR was self-contained.
• The proportionality standard of K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) is the latest layer of substantive review on top of the Maneka framework.

Union of India (1978) में, सर्वोच्च न्यायालय ने कहा कि अनुच्छेद 21 में 'प्रक्रिया' शब्द सही, न्यायसंगत और निष्पक्ष होना चाहिए — मनमाना, काल्पनिक या दमनकारी नहीं — प्रभावी रूप से एक ऐसे प्रावधान में सार्थक तर्कसंगतता पढ़ी जो अपने पाठ के अनुसार केवल प्रक्रियात्मक अनुपालन की आवश्यकता रखता था।
statement_analysis.reason: Maneka Gandhi (1978) ने A.K. Gopalan के उस दृष्टिकोण को खारिज कर दिया जो प्रत्येक मौलिक अधिकार को पृथक रूप से पढ़ता था। न्यायालय ने कहा कि अनुच्छेद 14, 19 और 21 को साथ में पढ़ा जाना चाहिए, और कोई भी प्रक्रिया जो किसी व्यक्ति के जीवन या स्वतंत्रता को छीनती है, उसे अनुच्छेद 14 के तहत तर्कसंगतता की आवश्यकताओं को पूरा करना चाहिए तथा अनुच्छेद 19 के तहत अधिकारों को अनुचित रूप से प्रतिबंधित नहीं करना चाहिए।

statement_analysis.statement: कथन 2: संविधान सभा ने जानबूझकर अनुच्छेद 21 में 'due process of law' की जगह 'procedure established by law' शब्दावली को इसलिए बदला क्योंकि डॉ. अम्बेडकर और अन्य को डर था कि 'due process' न्यायालयों को सामाजिक कल्याण कानूनों को खारिज करने के लिए अत्यधिक व्यापक अधिकार देगा — जो यह पुष्टि करता है कि भारत ने एक पूरी तरह प्रक्रियात्मक अनुच्छेद 21 का इरादा किया था जिसमें कोई सार्थक तत्व नहीं था।

solution.final_explanation:
अनुच्छेद 21 का इतिहास और विकास संवैधानिक कानून में सबसे अधिक परीक्षण किए जाने वाले विषयों में से एक है।

• कथन 1 — सही: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) अनुच्छेद 21 की व्याख्या में मील का पत्थर है। सर्वोच्च न्यायालय ने संकीर्ण A.K. Gopalan दृष्टिकोण (जिसमें प्रत्येक मौलिक अधिकार को अलग-थलग समझा जाता था) को खारिज कर दिया और कहा कि अनुच्छेद 14, 19, और 21 को एक संयुक्त ढांचे के रूप में पढ़ा जाना चाहिए। कोई भी प्रक्रिया जो जीवन या स्वतंत्रता छीनती है, वह सही, न्यायसंगत और तर्कसंगत होनी चाहिए — केवल औपचारिकता नहीं। इसने अनुच्छेद 21 में सार्थक प्रक्रिया के तत्वों को शामिल किया।
• कथन 2 — गलत: पहला भाग ऐतिहासिक रूप से सही है — संविधान सभा ने जानबूझकर 'procedure established by law' को अपनाया ताकि अमेरिकी शैली की सार्थक प्रक्रिया की समीक्षा से बचा जा सके। हालांकि, कथन 2 का निष्कर्ष — कि इस चयन ने स्थायी रूप से केवल प्रक्रियात्मक अनुच्छेद 21 की पुष्टि की — गलत है। Maneka Gandhi ने दिखाया कि न्यायिक व्याख्या मूल पाठ्य विकल्प से आगे बढ़ सकती है, और यह विकास संवैधानिक रूप से वैध है।

**मूल्य संवर्धन:**
• Maneka Gandhi के बाद, अनुच्छेद 21 के तहत जीवन का अधिकार आजीविका के अधिकार (Olga Tellis, 1985), स्वास्थ्य का अधिकार, शिक्षा का अधिकार (अनुच्छेद 21A के सम्मिलन से पहले), और निजता का अधिकार (Puttaswamy, 2017) शामिल करता है।
• A.K. Gopalan v. State of India (1950) पूर्व-Maneka प्राधिकरण था — जिसमें प्रत्येक मौलिक अधिकार को स्वतंत्र माना गया था।
• K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) का अनुपातिकता मानक Maneka ढांचे पर सार्थक समीक्षा की नवीनतम परत है।

statement_analysis.statement: All laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule, irrespective of the date of insertion, enjoy complete immunity from judicial scrutiny under Article 31B and can never be challenged for violating any Fundamental Right.
statement_analysis.reason: I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) held that laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 are subject to judicial review if they violate the Basic Structure or abridge Fundamental Rights under Articles 14, 19, and 21. Blanket immunity does not extend to post-1973 insertions.

statement_analysis.statement: Laws included in the Ninth Schedule before April 24, 1973 enjoy absolute immunity from judicial review, including from challenge on the ground that they violate Articles 14, 19, or 21.
statement_analysis.reason: I.R. Coelho specifically drew the line at April 24, 1973. Laws that were in the Ninth Schedule before that date — i.e., inserted before the Kesavananda Bharati judgment — retain their immunity from judicial review, including immunity from Part III challenges.

statement_analysis.statement: The cut-off date of April 24, 1973 adopted in I.R. Coelho corresponds to the date on which the Ninth Schedule itself was introduced into the Constitution through the First Constitutional Amendment.
statement_analysis.reason: April 24, 1973 is the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment — not the date the Ninth Schedule was introduced. The Ninth Schedule was introduced through the First Constitutional Amendment in 1951. The date is significant because the Basic Structure doctrine came into existence on April 24, 1973.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) which nominates only Statement 3 as incorrect is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statement 1 as wrong but mistakenly think Statement 3 is correct (confusing the 1951 introduction of the Schedule with the 1973 Kesavananda date) will choose an option that misses Statement 1.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Blanket immunity for ALL Ninth Schedule laws regardless of date — I.R. Coelho (2007) rejected this. Post-April 24, 1973 insertions are reviewable. Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Statement 2: Pre-April 24, 1973 laws enjoy absolute immunity — this is precisely what I.R. Coelho held. Statement 2 IS correct, so it is not among the incorrect ones.
Statement 3: The cut-off of April 24, 1973 corresponds to the Kesavananda Bharati judgment date, NOT the date the Ninth Schedule was introduced (1951). Statement 3 is NOT correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap in Statement 3 conflates two historically significant dates: 1951 (First Constitutional Amendment, Ninth Schedule introduced) and April 24, 1973 (Kesavananda Bharati judgment). Students who know both dates but have not made the specific connection between the I.R. Coelho cut-off and the Kesavananda date will choose the wrong anchor year.
solution.final_explanation:
The Ninth Schedule's immunity from judicial review is a carefully calibrated, date-dependent rule — not a blanket protection.

• Statement 1 — NOT correct: The I.R. Coelho (2007) nine-judge bench rejected the argument that Article 31B confers universal, perpetual immunity to all Ninth Schedule laws. Laws inserted after April 24, 1973 are reviewable if they violate the Basic Structure or abridge rights under Articles 14, 19, and 21.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Laws inserted before April 24, 1973 retain absolute immunity. I.R. Coelho held that the Basic Structure doctrine was not in existence before that date, so laws that preceded the doctrine cannot be retroactively subjected to it.
• Statement 3 — NOT correct: The cut-off date of April 24, 1973 is the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment — the day the Basic Structure doctrine was born. The Ninth Schedule itself was created by the First Constitutional Amendment of 1951 — a full 22 years earlier. The I.R. Coelho court chose April 24, 1973 because that is when Parliament's unlimited amending power was first judicially constrained.

**Value Addition:**
• As of I.R. Coelho, 284 Acts are listed in the Ninth Schedule — including land reform Acts, bank nationalisation Acts, and various State acts.
• The original rationale for the Ninth Schedule was to protect land reform laws from challenges under Articles 14 and 19 by zamindars — a post-independence agrarian reform imperative.
• Any law added to the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 must pass the Basic Structure test even though it is 'in the Ninth Schedule.'

• I.R. Coelho के अनुसार, नौवीं अनुसूची में 284 अधिनियम सूचीबद्ध हैं — जिनमें भूमि सुधार अधिनियम, बैंक राष्ट्रीयकरण अधिनियम, और विभिन्न राज्य अधिनियम शामिल हैं।

• 24 अप्रैल, 1973 के बाद नौवीं अनुसूची में जोड़ा गया कोई भी कानून मूलभूत संरचना परीक्षण से गुजरना होगा, भले ही वह 'नौवीं अनुसूची में हो।'

solution.concept_anchor: In Re Delhi Laws Act — permissible delegation and essential legislative function
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who know both the Delhi Laws Act case and the US non-delegation doctrine may assume the Indian case adopted the US doctrine, making R seem like a correct causal explanation of A.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Indian courts apply an 'excessive delegation' test, not a strict 'non-delegation doctrine.' The In Re Delhi Laws Act (1951) case held that essential legislative functions cannot be delegated, but Parliament may delegate non-essential functions. A is correct.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — R states the Indian Constitution 'expressly prohibits' delegation of legislative power. There is no such express prohibition in the Indian Constitution — unlike the US, where the non-delegation doctrine is judicially implied from the constitutional vesting of legislative power in Congress. The Indian Constitution has no equivalent express provision. R is incorrect.
Step 3: Causal link irrelevant since R is false.
A is correct, R is incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: R employs a plausible-fabrication technique: it states that the Indian Constitution 'expressly prohibits' delegation of legislative power. This is false — there is no such express prohibition. The restriction on excessive delegation in India is entirely judge-made, derived from the In Re Delhi Laws Act (1951) case and subsequent decisions. The US has a judicially implied non-delegation doctrine (from Article I); India has no equivalent explicit or implied textual provision — making the 'excessive delegation' test permissively applied. Students who know delegation is restricted in India may incorrectly assume this restriction has a constitutional text behind it.
solution.final_explanation:
The permissibility of legislative delegation is a fundamental question at the intersection of the separation of powers and parliamentary efficiency.

**Assertion (A):** Correct — In Re Delhi Laws Act (1951) — a seven-judge bench case — is India's foundational authority on delegated legislation. The Court held that Parliament can delegate non-essential legislative functions but cannot delegate 'essential legislative functions' — those that go to the core of policy-making. India's test is the 'excessive delegation' test, applied more permissively than the American non-delegation doctrine.

**Reason (R):** Incorrect — No provision in the Indian Constitution expressly prohibits the delegation of legislative power. The restriction is judge-made. Contrast with the US, where the non-delegation doctrine is implied from the vesting clauses of Article I (which vests all legislative power in Congress) — even then, it has been strictly applied only twice (1935). India's Constitution contains no equivalent vesting clause that could support a strict non-delegation reading.

A is correct, R is incorrect — option (c).

**Value Addition:**
• In the US, the non-delegation doctrine was most strictly applied in A.L.A. Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States (1935) — the last time a law was struck down on pure non-delegation grounds.
• Indian courts have permitted extremely wide delegation provided an 'intelligible policy' or 'standard' can be gathered from the parent Act.
• Procedural ultra vires (failure to follow mandatory consultation or laying requirements) is an additional independent ground for striking down delegated legislation in India.

formatted_presentation.display_text:
Assertion (A): Unlike the United States, where courts apply a strict non-delegation doctrine, Indian courts apply a more permissive 'excessive delegation' test — holding that Parliament may delegate non-essential legislative functions to executive authorities while retaining essential policy-making functions, as established in In Re Delhi Laws Act (1951).

Reason (R): The Indian Constitution expressly prohibits the delegation of legislative power by Parliament to the executive, and courts enforce this prohibition by striking down any delegated legislation that exceeds the power granted by the parent Act.

(a) Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A
(b) Both A and R are correct, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
(c) A is correct but R is incorrect
(d) A is incorrect but R is correct

चरण 3: कारण अप्रासंगिक है क्योंकि R गलत है।

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: R एक संभावित-निर्मित तकनीक का उपयोग करता है: यह कहता है कि भारतीय संविधान संसद द्वारा विधायी शक्ति के प्रतिनिधित्व को 'स्पष्ट रूप से प्रतिबंधित' करता है। यह गलत है — ऐसा कोई स्पष्ट प्रतिबंध नहीं है। भारत में अत्यधिक प्रतिनिधित्व पर प्रतिबंध पूरी तरह से न्यायाधीश निर्मित है, जो In Re Delhi Laws Act (1951) मामले और बाद के निर्णयों से निकला है। अमेरिका में न्यायिक रूप से व्युत्पन्न गैर-प्रतिनिधित्व सिद्धांत (अनुच्छेद I से) है; भारत में ऐसा कोई स्पष्ट या निहित प्रावधान नहीं है — इसलिए 'अत्यधिक प्रतिनिधित्व' परीक्षण अधिक उदारता से लागू होता है। जो छात्र जानते हैं कि भारत में प्रतिनिधित्व प्रतिबंधित है, वे गलत तरीके से मान सकते हैं कि इस प्रतिबंध के पीछे कोई संवैधानिक पाठ है।
solution.final_explanation:
विधायी प्रतिनिधित्व की अनुमति शक्ति, शक्तियों के पृथक्करण और संसदीय दक्षता के संगम पर एक मौलिक प्रश्न है।

**कथन (A):** सही — In Re Delhi Laws Act (1951) — सात न्यायाधीशों की पीठ का मामला — भारत में प्रतिनिधि विधान का आधार है। न्यायालय ने कहा कि संसद गैर-आवश्यक विधायी कार्य सौंप सकती है लेकिन 'आवश्यक विधायी कार्य' — जो नीति-निर्माण के मूल में जाते हैं — सौंप नहीं सकती। भारत का परीक्षण 'अत्यधिक प्रतिनिधित्व' परीक्षण है, जो अमेरिकी गैर-प्रतिनिधित्व सिद्धांत की तुलना में अधिक उदार है।

**कारण (R):** गलत — भारतीय संविधान में संसद द्वारा विधायी शक्ति के प्रतिनिधित्व पर कोई स्पष्ट प्रतिबंध नहीं है। यह प्रतिबंध न्यायाधीश निर्मित है। अमेरिका के विपरीत, जहां गैर-प्रतिनिधित्व सिद्धांत अनुच्छेद I के अधिकारों से व्युत्पन्न है (जो सभी विधायी शक्ति कांग्रेस को देता है) — और तब भी इसे केवल दो बार सख्ती से लागू किया गया (1935)। भारत के संविधान में ऐसा कोई समकक्ष प्रावधान नहीं है जो सख्त गैर-प्रतिनिधित्व व्याख्या का समर्थन करे।

A सही है, R गलत है — विकल्प (c)।

**मूल्य संवर्धन:**
• अमेरिका में गैर-प्रतिनिधित्व सिद्धांत को सबसे सख्ती से A.L.A. Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States (1935) में लागू किया गया था — जब अंतिम बार किसी कानून को केवल गैर-प्रतिनिधित्व के आधार पर रद्द किया गया।
• भारतीय न्यायालयों ने अत्यधिक व्यापक प्रतिनिधित्व की अनुमति दी है बशर्ते मूल अधिनियम से 'बोधगम्य नीति' या 'मानक' निकाला जा सके।
• प्रक्रिया संबंधी अल्ट्रा वायर्स (अनिवार्य परामर्श या प्रस्तुतिकरण आवश्यकताओं का पालन न करना) भारत में प्रतिनिधि विधान को रद्द करने का एक स्वतंत्र आधार है।

solution.concept_anchor: High Court writ jurisdiction under Article 226 — cause of action and territorial limits
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because it invokes the plausible principle that the court with the widest reach should take the case — students who know the Supreme Court has all-India jurisdiction may choose this as a shortcut, not knowing the High Court territorial jurisdiction rule.
elimination_logic: Identify the governing rule: Article 226 — a High Court can issue writs if (a) the cause of action arises wholly or partly within its territorial jurisdiction, OR (b) the respondent is located within its territorial jurisdiction.

Apply to the scenario: The respondent (company headquarters) is in Mumbai — Maharashtra High Court. The cause of action (dismissal, employment contract) arose in Bengaluru — Karnataka High Court. Neither the Madras High Court nor any other court has jurisdiction.
The petitioner lives in Chennai — but residence of the petitioner does NOT confer jurisdiction on the local High Court.
Option (c) correctly identifies that the Karnataka High Court (cause of action) or the Bombay High Court (respondent's location) has jurisdiction — the Madras High Court does not.
Select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap places the petitioner in Chennai (Madras High Court jurisdiction) while the cause of action and the respondent are in different states. Students who apply the intuitive rule 'you file a case where you live' will choose Madras High Court — the wrong answer. The correct rule under Ambica Industries is: jurisdiction attaches where the cause of action arises OR where the respondent is located, not where the petitioner resides.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 226's territorial jurisdiction for High Courts is determined by specific legal rules, not by the petitioner's place of residence.

**Governing rule (Ambica Industries v. Commissioner of Central Excise):** A High Court can exercise writ jurisdiction under Article 226 if — (a) the cause of action arises wholly or partly within its territory, OR (b) the respondent authority or person is situated within its territory. The petitioner's residence is irrelevant.

**Applying to the scenario:**
- Cause of action (dismissal, breach of employment terms): arose in Bengaluru → Karnataka High Court has jurisdiction.
- Respondent (company headquarters): Mumbai → Bombay High Court has jurisdiction.
- Petitioner's residence: Chennai — this does NOT confer jurisdiction on the Madras High Court.

• Option (a): Incorrect — The Supreme Court under Article 32 can be approached only for enforcement of Fundamental Rights. An employment dispute against a private company (unless a 'state' under Article 12) would not normally be maintainable under Article 32. Moreover, courts do not automatically transfer to the highest forum.
• Option (b): Incorrect — The Madras High Court has no connection to the cause of action or to the respondent's location. Petitioner's residence in Chennai is insufficient.
• Option (c): Correct — Karnataka High Court (where the cause of action arose) or Bombay High Court (where the respondent is headquartered) are the appropriate forums.
• Option (d): Incorrect — There is no rule requiring a petitioner to approach the court where the contract was originally signed; cause of action and respondent location govern jurisdiction.

**Value Addition:**
• A cause of action can arise in multiple states (e.g., a contract signed in Delhi, breach occurring in Mumbai) — both High Courts would have jurisdiction in that case.
• Article 226 jurisdiction extends to any government, authority, or person — even private entities performing public functions.
• The Supreme Court can transfer cases between High Courts under Article 139A.

(d) She must file before the Telangana High Court at Hyderabad since the original employment contract was executed there

परिदृश्य पर लागू करें: प्रतिवादी (कंपनी मुख्यालय) मुंबई में है — महाराष्ट्र उच्च न्यायालय। कार्यवाही का कारण (बर्खास्तगी, रोजगार अनुबंध) बेंगलुरु में उत्पन्न हुआ — कर्नाटक उच्च न्यायालय। न मद्रास उच्च न्यायालय का और न ही किसी अन्य न्यायालय का क्षेत्राधिकार है।
याचिकाकर्ता चेन्नई में रहता है — लेकिन याचिकाकर्ता का निवास स्थानीय उच्च न्यायालय को क्षेत्राधिकार प्रदान नहीं करता।
विकल्प (c) सही रूप से पहचानता है कि कर्नाटक उच्च न्यायालय (जहाँ कार्यवाही का कारण उत्पन्न हुआ) या बॉम्बे उच्च न्यायालय (जहाँ प्रतिवादी स्थित है) का क्षेत्राधिकार है — मद्रास उच्च न्यायालय का नहीं।
विकल्प (c) चुनें।
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: भौगोलिक-स्थानांतरण भ्रम याचिकाकर्ता को चेन्नई (मद्रास उच्च न्यायालय के क्षेत्राधिकार) में रखता है जबकि कार्यवाही का कारण और प्रतिवादी अलग-अलग राज्यों में हैं। जो छात्र सहज नियम 'जहाँ आप रहते हैं वहाँ मामला दर्ज करें' लागू करते हैं, वे मद्रास उच्च न्यायालय चुनेंगे — जो गलत उत्तर है। अम्बिका इंडस्ट्रीज के तहत सही नियम है: क्षेत्राधिकार उस स्थान पर होता है जहाँ कार्यवाही का कारण उत्पन्न होता है या जहाँ प्रतिवादी स्थित है, न कि जहाँ याचिकाकर्ता रहता है।
solution.final_explanation:
अनुच्छेद 226 के तहत उच्च न्यायालयों का क्षेत्राधिकार याचिकाकर्ता के निवास स्थान से नहीं, बल्कि विशिष्ट कानूनी नियमों से निर्धारित होता है।

**शासन नियम (Ambica Industries v. Commissioner of Central Excise):** एक उच्च न्यायालय अनुच्छेद 226 के तहत रिट क्षेत्राधिकार तब प्रयोग कर सकता है जब — (a) कार्यवाही का कारण पूरी तरह या आंशिक रूप से उसके क्षेत्र में उत्पन्न होता है, या (b) प्रतिवादी प्राधिकारी या व्यक्ति उसके क्षेत्र में स्थित हो। याचिकाकर्ता का निवास स्थान अप्रासंगिक है।

**परिदृश्य पर लागू करना:**
- कार्यवाही का कारण (बर्खास्तगी, रोजगार शर्तों का उल्लंघन): बेंगलुरु में उत्पन्न → कर्नाटक उच्च न्यायालय का क्षेत्राधिकार।
- प्रतिवादी (कंपनी मुख्यालय): मुंबई → बॉम्बे उच्च न्यायालय का क्षेत्राधिकार।
- याचिकाकर्ता का निवास: चेन्नई — यह मद्रास उच्च न्यायालय को क्षेत्राधिकार प्रदान नहीं करता।

• विकल्प (a): गलत — अनुच्छेद 32 के तहत सुप्रीम कोर्ट केवल मौलिक अधिकारों के प्रवर्तन के लिए ही पहुंच योग्य है। एक निजी कंपनी के विरुद्ध रोजगार विवाद (जब तक कि वह अनुच्छेद 12 के तहत 'राज्य' न हो) सामान्यतः अनुच्छेद 32 के तहत नहीं चलाया जा सकता। इसके अलावा, न्यायालय स्वतः मामलों को उच्चतम मंच पर स्थानांतरित नहीं करते।
• विकल्प (b): गलत — मद्रास उच्च न्यायालय का कार्यवाही के कारण या प्रतिवादी के स्थान से कोई संबंध नहीं है। याचिकाकर्ता का चेन्नई में निवास अपर्याप्त है।
• विकल्प (c): सही — कर्नाटक उच्च न्यायालय (जहाँ कार्यवाही का कारण उत्पन्न हुआ) या बॉम्बे उच्च न्यायालय (जहाँ प्रतिवादी मुख्यालय है) उपयुक्त न्यायालय हैं।
• विकल्प (d): गलत — ऐसा कोई नियम नहीं है कि याचिकाकर्ता को उस न्यायालय में जाना चाहिए जहाँ अनुबंध मूल रूप से किया गया था; क्षेत्राधिकार कार्यवाही के कारण और प्रतिवादी के स्थान से निर्धारित होता है।

**मूल्यवर्धन:**
• कार्यवाही का कारण कई राज्यों में उत्पन्न हो सकता है (जैसे, दिल्ली में अनुबंध किया गया, मुंबई में उल्लंघन हुआ) — उस स्थिति में दोनों उच्च न्यायालयों का क्षेत्राधिकार होगा।
• अनुच्छेद 226 का क्षेत्राधिकार किसी भी सरकार, प्राधिकारी या व्यक्ति तक विस्तृत होता है — यहाँ तक कि वे निजी संस्थाएँ भी जो सार्वजनिक कार्य करती हैं।
• सुप्रीम कोर्ट अनुच्छेद 139A के तहत उच्च न्यायालयों के बीच मामले स्थानांतरित कर सकता है।

चेन्नई (तमिलनाडु) में आधारित एक निजी क्षेत्र की कर्मचारी को उसकी सेवा से बर्खास्त कर दिया गया, जिसकी कंपनी का मुख्यालय मुंबई (महाराष्ट्र) में है। बर्खास्तगी कंपनी की बेंगलुरु (कर्नाटक) शाखा में की गई जहाँ वह तैनात थी। वह बर्खास्तगी को रिट याचिका के माध्यम से चुनौती देना चाहती है। उसका रोजगार अनुबंध मूल रूप से हैदराबाद में किया गया था। संविधान के अनुच्छेद 226 के तहत वह सबसे उपयुक्त रूप से कहाँ रिट याचिका दायर कर सकती है?

(b) वह मद्रास उच्च न्यायालय में याचिका दायर कर सकती है क्योंकि वह सामान्यतः चेन्नई में रहती है और यह उसके लिए सबसे सुविधाजनक होगा

solution.concept_anchor: Kesavananda Bharati — bench composition, majority, date, and basic structure scope

statement_analysis.statement: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) was decided by a 13-judge constitutional bench with a 7:6 majority.
statement_analysis.reason: The Kesavananda Bharati case was heard by the largest bench in Indian judicial history — 13 judges — and was decided by a narrow 7:6 majority in favour of the Basic Structure doctrine.

statement_analysis.statement: The Kesavananda Bharati judgment held that Parliament's power to amend the Constitution is unlimited as long as the amendment is passed with the required two-thirds majority in both Houses.
statement_analysis.reason: Precisely the opposite is true: Kesavananda held that Parliament's amending power under Article 368 is limited by the Basic Structure of the Constitution — it cannot amend away the Basic Structure regardless of the majority. The two-thirds majority is a procedural requirement, not a substantive licence for unlimited amendment.

statement_analysis.statement: The Kesavananda Bharati judgment was pronounced on April 24, 1973 — a date that serves as the temporal cut-off in I.R. Coelho (2007) for determining the immunity of Ninth Schedule laws.
statement_analysis.reason: April 24, 1973 is the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment. I.R. Coelho (2007) used this date as the cut-off: laws inserted in the Ninth Schedule before this date enjoy absolute immunity; those inserted after are subject to judicial review on Basic Structure and Part III grounds.

statement_analysis.statement: The Basic Structure doctrine as articulated in Kesavananda Bharati extends to review of ordinary legislation, enabling courts to strike down a parliamentary Act if it undermines an identified Basic Structure element.
statement_analysis.reason: Basic Structure is a doctrine limiting Parliament's power under Article 368 (constitutional amendments), not its ordinary legislative power. Ordinary legislation is tested against Fundamental Rights in Part III. Basic Structure is NOT a direct ground for striking down ordinary legislation.

solution.strong_distractor: c — 'Only three' is a strong distractor because students who accept Statement 4 as correct (confusing Basic Structure's domain as universal) will count three correct statements and choose (c).
elimination_logic: Statement 1: 13-judge bench, 7:6 majority in Kesavananda Bharati — correct historical fact. Correct.
Statement 2: Kesavananda held Parliament's amending power is LIMITED by Basic Structure — the claim of 'unlimited power' is precisely what was rejected. Incorrect.
Statement 3: April 24, 1973 = Kesavananda date = I.R. Coelho cut-off. Correct.
Statement 4: Basic Structure applies to Article 368 amendments, NOT to ordinary legislation. Incorrect.
Two statements (1 and 3) are correct — select option (b) 'Only two'.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 4 uses the partial-truth technique: Basic Structure is indeed the supreme constitutional standard, and courts do use it in reviewing constitutional amendments. The trap is extending this domain to ordinary legislation. A student who knows Basic Structure is supremely important but has not internalised its precise jurisdictional limit (Article 368 amendments only) will mark Statement 4 as correct and over-count.
solution.final_explanation:
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) is arguably the most important judgment in Indian constitutional history.

| Statement | Verdict |
|---|---|
| 1. 13-judge bench, 7:6 majority | Correct |
| 2. Parliament has unlimited amending power if two-thirds majority obtained | Incorrect |
| 3. April 24, 1973 = Kesavananda date = I.R. Coelho cut-off | Correct |
| 4. Basic Structure applies to ordinary legislation as well | Incorrect |

Only two statements are correct.

**Value Addition:**
• The Kesavananda majority opinion was compiled by Justice H.R. Khanna's synthesis note — without it the precise majority position would have been unclear given 13 individual opinions.
• Chief Justice S.M. Sikri delivered the judgment on April 24, 1973, his last day in office — an iconic constitutional moment.
• In the immediate aftermath, the government under Indira Gandhi superseded three senior judges (Shelat, Grover, Hegde) who had formed part of the Kesavananda majority when appointing the next Chief Justice — a controversy that defined the judiciary-executive relationship for decades.

दो कथन (1 और 3) सही हैं — विकल्प (b) 'केवल दो' चुनें।

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap pairs the Nabam Rebia holding (conflict of interest — Speaker with pending removal notice cannot decide disqualification) with Kihoto Hollohan (which is more famous). solution.final_explanation:
The Tenth Schedule has produced a layered body of judicial review jurisprudence, with different cases contributing different rules.

• Option (a) — Correct: Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker, Arunachal Pradesh (2016) is the controlling authority for the specific rule that a Speaker who is facing a pending notice for their own removal under Article 179 cannot decide disqualification petitions under the Tenth Schedule. The Court held this would be a conflict of interest that compromises the fairness of the adjudicatory process.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) established that (a) the Speaker acts as a tribunal under the Tenth Schedule, (b) Speaker's decisions are judicially reviewable on limited grounds, and (c) Paragraph 7 (which barred judicial review) violated the Basic Structure. It did not address the conflict-of-interest scenario.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Rajendra Singh Rana v. Swami Prasad Maurya (2007) dealt with deemed disqualification and merger provisions under the Tenth Schedule — not with Speaker's conflict of interest.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Keisham Meghachandra Singh v. Speaker, Manipur (2020) further extended Nabam Rebia principles and held that Speakers should ideally decide disqualification cases within three months — but this is a different rule.

**Value Addition:**
• The logical foundation of Nabam Rebia is natural justice — no one should be a judge in their own cause (nemo judex in causa sua).
• Multiple states have witnessed political crises involving this rule: Arunachal Pradesh (2016), Karnataka (2019), Manipur.
• The 91st Constitutional Amendment (2003) amended the Tenth Schedule to remove the provision that exempted merger of at least one-third of a party's members from disqualification — now the threshold is two-thirds.

solution.concept_anchor: Finality clauses — Kihoto Hollohan logic applied to Article 110(3) and Article 74(2)

statement_analysis.statement: The principle established in Kihoto Hollohan (1992) — that a 'finality clause' in a constitutional provision does not completely oust the power of judicial review — has been applied by courts as a persuasive argument for holding that the Speaker's certification of a Money Bill under Article 110(3) may also be subject to limited judicial review.
statement_analysis.reason: In Kihoto Hollohan, the Court struck down Paragraph 7 of the Tenth Schedule (which was a finality/ouster clause) as violating the Basic Structure — since judicial review is a Basic Structure element. The same logic has been invoked in arguments about Article 110(3)'s 'finality' — though the question remains constitutionally unresolved, pending the Rojer Mathew larger bench reference.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 74(2)'s bar on courts inquiring into ministerial advice to the President is absolute and cannot be overcome even if it is alleged that the advice was tainted by mala fides or constituted a fraud on the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 74(2) is an express bar — courts cannot inquire into what advice was given or whether advice was given at all. While the bar is very strong, Indian courts have not definitively ruled on whether extreme cases (fraud on the Constitution) could override it. The statement that it 'cannot be overcome even if fraud is alleged' states a broader proposition than has been conclusively settled, and standard constitutional doctrine treats it as very strong but not necessarily impervious to every challenge.

statement_analysis.statement: The Supreme Court, in applying the Kihoto Hollohan doctrine, held that courts always retain residual power to review decisions of constitutional authorities even when an explicit finality clause exists in the Constitution, making no constitutional provision wholly immune from judicial scrutiny.
statement_analysis.reason: Kihoto Hollohan held that the finality clause in Paragraph 7 of the Tenth Schedule was invalid because it violated the Basic Structure. However, this does not mean ALL finality clauses in the Constitution are invalid. Article 74(2) is an express textual bar that courts have consistently respected. The proposition that 'no constitutional provision is wholly immune from judicial scrutiny' overstates the Kihoto Hollohan holding.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Wait: options (a)-(d) must be constructed. Option listing Statement 1 and 2 as correct would be the distractor. For this question the structure gives: Statement 1 correct, Statements 2 and 3 incorrect. So only Statement 1 is correct — option (a). The strong distractor is option (c) '1 and 3 only' because Statement 3 sounds like a broad correct principle derived from Kihoto Hollohan and students may accept it.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Kihoto Hollohan's logic (finality clauses do not completely oust review) has been used in arguments about Article 110(3) Money Bill certification — this is a documented and unsettled constitutional argument. Statement 1 is correct.

Statement 2: Article 74(2) is described as absolutely impervious to any challenge including fraud allegations. This overstates — while very strong, the outer limits of Article 74(2) are not conclusively settled. Statement 2 is an overstatement and is incorrect.

Statement 3: Extends Kihoto Hollohan to say 'no constitutional provision is wholly immune from judicial scrutiny.' This universalisation is incorrect — Article 74(2), Article 105(2) create zones genuinely shielded from review. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Only Statement 1 is correct — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 deploys a scope-extension trap on the Kihoto Hollohan doctrine: students who correctly understand Kihoto as a Basic Structure victory over ouster clauses may overgeneralise it as establishing that no provision can completely oust review. This is incorrect — specific express constitutional bars (like Article 74(2)) remain effective. The correct position is that ouster clauses inserted by Parliament (even in the Constitution via Article 368) are suspect under Basic Structure, but textually embedded non-justiciability provisions in the original Constitution retain their force.
solution.final_explanation:
The relationship between finality clauses and judicial review is an evolving area of constitutional jurisprudence.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Kihoto Hollohan (1992) established that a finality/ouster clause inserted by Parliament (in the Tenth Schedule) could be struck down if it violated the Basic Structure. This logic has been cited in arguments challenging Article 110(3)'s 'finality' for Money Bill certification — and the Rojer Mathew reference (2019) is pending on precisely this question.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 74(2)'s bar is very strong and courts have consistently respected it. However, describing it as 'absolute and cannot be overcome even if fraud is alleged' states a broader proposition than has been definitively settled. Constitutional doctrine distinguishes between express bars that are textually embedded versus judicially created finality — the former are more robust.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Kihoto Hollohan does not establish that no constitutional provision can ever completely oust review. Article 74(2) is a case where courts have accepted the bar. The proper principle is narrower: Parliament cannot, via Article 368, insert ouster clauses that destroy the Basic Structure element of judicial review; but some original constitutional provisions do create legitimate non-justiciable zones.

**Value Addition:**
• The distinction between 'ouster clause inserted by Parliament' (challengeable under Basic Structure) and 'non-justiciability embedded in original Constitution' (stronger footing) is a nuanced but testable area.
• L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997) held that even the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and High Courts cannot be ousted by Parliament — this is a Basic Structure element.
• The Rojer Mathew reference on Money Bill certification reviewability is one of the most watched constitutional questions of the current decade.

The correct position is that ouster clauses inserted by Parliament (even in the Constitution via Article 368) are suspect under Basic Structure, but textually embedded non-justiciability provisions in the original Constitution retain their force.
solution.final_explanation:
The relationship between finality clauses and judicial review is an evolving area of constitutional jurisprudence.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Kihoto Hollohan (1992) established that a finality/ouster clause inserted by Parliament (in the Tenth Schedule) could be struck down if it violated the Basic Structure. This logic has been cited in arguments challenging Article 110(3)'s 'finality' for Money Bill certification — and the Rojer Mathew reference (2019) is pending on precisely this question.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 74(2)'s bar is very strong and courts have consistently respected it. However, describing it as 'absolute and cannot be overcome even if fraud is alleged' states a broader proposition than has been definitively settled. Constitutional doctrine distinguishes between express bars that are textually embedded versus judicially created finality — the former are more robust.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Kihoto Hollohan does not establish that no constitutional provision can ever completely oust review. Article 74(2) is a case where courts have accepted the bar. The proper principle is narrower: Parliament cannot, via Article 368, insert ouster clauses that destroy the Basic Structure element of judicial review; but some original constitutional provisions do create legitimate non-justiciable zones.

**Value Addition:**
• The distinction between 'ouster clause inserted by Parliament' (challengeable under Basic Structure) and 'non-justiciability embedded in original Constitution' (stronger footing) is a nuanced but testable area.
• L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997) held that even the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and High Courts cannot be ousted by Parliament — this is a Basic Structure element.
• The Rojer Mathew reference on Money Bill certification reviewability is one of the most watched constitutional questions of the current decade.

formatted_presentation.display_text:
संवैधानिक प्रावधानों में अंतिमता क्लॉज और उनके न्यायिक समीक्षा से संबंध के संदर्भ में, निम्नलिखित कथनों पर विचार करें:

1. Kihoto Hollohan (1992) में स्थापित सिद्धांत — कि किसी संवैधानिक प्रावधान में 'अंतिमता क्लॉज' न्यायिक समीक्षा के अधिकार को पूरी तरह समाप्त नहीं करता — को न्यायालयों द्वारा एक प्रेरक तर्क के रूप में लागू किया गया है कि अनुच्छेद 110(3) के तहत स्पीकर द्वारा मनी बिल के प्रमाणन पर भी सीमित न्यायिक समीक्षा हो सकती है।
2. अनुच्छेद 74(2) के तहत राष्ट्रपति को दिए गए मंत्रीमंडल के परामर्श की जांच करने में न्यायालयों पर लगाया गया प्रतिबंध पूर्ण है और इसे इस बात के बावजूद भी पार नहीं किया जा सकता कि परामर्श में दुर्भावना या संविधान के साथ धोखाधड़ी का आरोप लगाया गया हो।
3. सुप्रीम कोर्ट ने Kihoto Hollohan सिद्धांत को लागू करते हुए यह कहा कि न्यायालयों के पास सदैव संवैधानिक प्राधिकरणों के निर्णयों की समीक्षा करने की अवशिष्ट शक्ति रहती है, भले ही संविधान में स्पष्ट अंतिमता क्लॉज मौजूद हो, जिससे कोई भी संवैधानिक प्रावधान न्यायिक जांच से पूरी तरह मुक्त नहीं होता।

उपरोक्त में से कौन-सा/से कथन सही है/हैं?

(a) केवल 1
(b) केवल 2
(c) केवल 1 और 3
(d) 1, 2 और 3
